correctness.rationale: The child-failure fixed point x=p_rho+int_{m0}^rho f(u)(1-exp[-kappa mu(u)x])du follows by independent marks, all-generation branching and Poisson generating functions. Its Lipschitz constant is at most n=kappa E(mu)<1; x tends to zero and Taylor expansion uniformly in bounded productivity gives x~p/(1-n). Poisson root offspring then give F=1-exp[-kappa mu(rho)x], and positive endpoint density gives p~f(M)(M-rho). Independent quadrature and root-finding reproduced the coefficient under a strictly subcritical parameter set; no finite computation supports critical n=1.

originality.rationale: FAIL: Saichev and Sornette (2005) already derive the exact ALL-GENERATION maximal-aftershock probability from a Poisson-marked ETAS generating functional (equations 31-35), not merely an expected cascade count. Their formula is structurally valid for arbitrary independent child-mark laws, including finite truncated laws; Sornette and Werner (2005) explicitly give the normalized finite-upper-cutoff Gutenberg-Richter law and mean total progeny. Substituting this established law into the established fixed point and taking its derivative at an endpoint produces precisely this linear coefficient by a routine first-order expansion, with no new structural lemma. The earlier paper also explicitly gives a large-threshold tail factor 1/(1-n) in Eq.44. Although this exact finite-endpoint numerical coefficient is not printed there, the submitted result is a mechanically implied corollary of stronger prior distributional work, not an original theorem. No scientific repair was staged or claimed.
residual_risks: Prior paper specializes to unbounded Gutenberg-Richter marks in its numerical plots; structural generating-functional identity applies to any independent normalized mark law, as shown algebraically.
No claim of a printed identical finite cutoff coefficient: implication is mathematical rather than literal.
At n=1 the derivative argument breaks down; no conclusion is claimed.

value.rationale: The finite magnitude-endpoint slope is a physically meaningful boundary statistic: a hard upper cutoff necessarily destroys magnitude-independent foreshock probability and supplies a quantitative model comparison. It can be useful for interpreting ETAS within a fixed subcritical regime, even though it is an elementary consequence of prior generating-function theory.
